title: Last Light
subtitle: Friday 11 to Sunday 13 October 1974: Seventy Good Years, Seven Houses, a Live Broadcast and the Cold Hole at Sunset

setting.name: Harvest Days, the Hollow and the Cold Hole, 11 to 13 October 1974
setting.description: The seventieth Harvest Days. Main Street is hung with bunting and red kerchiefs; the fairgrounds by the north branch of the creek have a pavilion with long tables for six hundred, a pie tent, a beer tent run by the volunteer firemen, a tractor-pull track, a bandstand, and the Channel 8 news van with its mast up, booked to go live at six on Saturday. Friday is the parade (the high school band, the fire truck, a float from every church and club, antique tractors, the co-op's new grain dryer on a flatbed, and the Harvest Queen, by tradition a grandmother: this year Elsie Brandvold), and the co-op open house. Saturday is the tractor pull at ten, the pie auction at two, the supper at five, the TV at six, and at last light, 6:21 p.m., the walk to the rim of the Hollow 'to see the sunset'. The town is Closed and smiling. The guest, now a player character (or Dawn, if she was caught; or Pastor Tove), is the town's guest of honour, with a seat at the head table and a place in the walk. The party has a day and a half to bring a living member of each of the seven houses to the Cold Hole at last light with the Book, and to keep the guest from walking down to it alone. The Landlord has waited seventy years for this supper, and it knows something is wrong.
setting.atmosphere: A county fair at the end of the world. Bright October sun, red maples, a brass band, the smell of brats and kettle corn and diesel, children with balloons, old men in seed caps judging tractors, teenagers sneaking beers behind the fire truck, the TV reporter doing her hair in the van's mirror. Everyone is happy, or pretending; everyone is wearing a red kerchief. Under it, the town is holding its breath. Let the festival be genuinely joyful and genuinely sinister at once. Then sunset: the light going gold and long, the crowd walking out the Fossum lane between walls of corn toward the rim, a bagpipe or a fiddle playing, and the Cold Hole breathing out white below, faster than it ever has. Then dark, and the cold, and seven people reading from a book.

keyLocations.name: The Harvest Days Grounds
keyLocations.description: The fairgrounds on the flats by the north branch of the creek, below the village: the pavilion (a long open shed with a concrete floor and tables for six hundred, where the supper is served at five), the pie tent, the beer tent, the bandstand, the tractor-pull track, a midway of three rides from a carnival out of Tomah, the Channel 8 van parked by the bandstand with its mast up and a cable run to a camera on a tripod, and the running creek along the north side, which is the edge of the Landlord's land.
features: The head table in the pavilion: the board, the Harvest Queen, the pastor, and a chair with a red kerchief laid on the plate: the guest's
The bread: a basket of Arvid's Harvest Supper loaves on every table, baked from the first grain of the 1974 harvest, and the toast 'to our guest'
The creek along the grounds' north edge, twenty yards from the pavilion: the wall
encounters: Six hundred townsfolk, kind and watchful
Bonnie Sedlak and Xavier Boone of Channel 8
Arnie Fossum's men keeping close to the guest, smiling, all day
secrets: The town's plan for the guest (core, from Rolf, Elsie or channel 14): the guest eats the supper ('took supper', for the Book), and at 6:10 the whole town walks out the Fossum lane to the rim with the guest at the front between Arnie and Marit, 'to see the sunset'; at the rim, the guest is left to walk down. The town does not push anyone. It has never had to. The bread and the call do it.

If the guest does not eat the Harvest Supper bread, the Book's line cannot be completed ('took supper' must be written), and the Landlord's call is weaker: the guest has advantage on every WIS save against Calling the Guest. The town knows this and will try very hard, and very kindly, to get one slice into them.

keyLocations.name: The Kubicek House and Gary's Clinic
keyLocations.description: Dr. Arlen Kubicek's white frame house on Church Street, with his practice in the front parlour; and across the alley his son Gary's veterinary clinic in a converted garage, with a sign painted by his daughters, KUBICEK ANIMAL HOSPITAL, and a kennel run. Gary, 26, is a big, cheerful, sunburned vet who does the town's cattle and dogs, plays first base for the Ridge Inn's softball team and has a wife, Carol, and two little girls. He had leukemia at ten and went into a remission that the Mayo Clinic wrote a paper about. He does not know.
features: Gary's office: a framed copy of the Mayo paper, 'An Unexplained Remission', 1959, that his father gave him on his twenty-first birthday without saying why
Dr. Kubicek's parlour: the bottle of phenobarbital; thirty years of 'fit to travel' notes in carbon
encounters: Dr. Arlen Kubicek, 66
Gary Kubicek, 26
secrets: LOWELL (the hardest conversation in the campaign): he has to be told what saved him, and that the price was a stranger a year, and that his father knew. Persuasion DC 15, or the Book's 1958 line (a hitchhiker from Iowa, 'Paid') and his father's face. He takes it badly, then well. He is a decent man. 'I've had sixteen years. They had none.' He will speak for the house of Kubicek. GM: the bargain's end will not take back his health (the rules say nothing of it, and the GM never adds a rule); but Gary does not know that, and neither does the party, and he chooses anyway.
DR. KUBICEK: he will not speak against it, and he will not stand in Gary's way. If Gary goes to the Cold Hole, his father goes with him, and stands behind him, and holds his shoulders while he reads.

keyLocations.name: The Hollow Fork State Bank
keyLocations.description: Red brick, 1911, a marble counter, a walk-in vault with a hundred and forty families' notes in it, and upstairs Marit Lunde's office with its view of Main Street and the elevator. Her son Kjell, 30, the bank's loan officer, has the office across the hall. He wears his red kerchief in his pocket, not at his throat.
features: Marit's desk: the co-op loan file, $1.2 million; a ledger of the farm notes; a photograph of her late husband Anders Lunde III
Kjell's desk: a Peace Corps poster and an application to a bank in Minneapolis, unsent
encounters: Marit Lunde, 54
Kjell Lunde, 30
secrets: MARIT (the hardest keeper): she will not speak. Not for anything. 'I have a hundred and forty families in that vault. You want me to trade them for one stranger.' She cannot be talked round in a day; a party that tries hard and honestly (Persuasion DC 18) gets only this: she will not stop Kjell.

KJELL (core): he has known since he was eighteen and has hated it since he was eighteen and has never had the courage. Persuasion DC 12, or the Book, or the back room. He will speak for the house of Lunde. He asks the party to be there when he tells his mother.

keyLocations.name: The High Bridge at Winona
keyLocations.description: The Mississippi high bridge between Winona, Minnesota, and the Wisconsin shore: a steel cantilever span over a half mile of brown water, barges, islands and bluffs. Einar Aldahl has not crossed it in twenty-three years. On Friday, Emil Pospisil's eastbound Greyhound crosses it at 10:50 a.m. on its way to Hollow Fork at 11:40; or the party can drive over and fetch him.
features: Emil Pospisil's bus, which the town has cancelled at Hollow Fork and which comes anyway
encounters: Einar Aldahl, 79
Emil Pospisil, 52
secrets: EINAR (core, if Sylvie Aldahl asks him, or anyone tells him that the town wrote a living person's name after Dawn got out; Persuasion DC 14 otherwise): he will come. Crossing the bridge is a fear check DC 15 for him (he has advantage with Sylvie beside him). He rides with his father's red kerchief in his fist. 'If I'm going to be any use, I'd better do it before I'm dead.' If he will not come, Sylvie can speak for the Aldahls by blood.

EMIL (core): the town called the Greyhound depot to cancel the Hollow Fork stop for the festival. Emil stops anyway, at 11:40 Friday and at 4:10, and will carry anyone out who wants to go: Dawn, a frightened outsider, the TV crew's tapes. He will not leave the bus. He keeps the engine running.

keyLocations.name: The Rim and the Switchback
keyLocations.description: The Fossum lane between walls of standing corn to the rim, Ingeborg's stone house in its lilacs, and from the rim a switchback farm track down the side of the Hollow through birches and fir, past the bench where the Old Union Church leans, down the cold slope of mossy broken rock, to the coulee floor. Half a mile, ten minutes walking down by daylight; by last light, with the cold coming up, longer.
features: The rim at sunset: the whole town, six hundred people, standing in the stubble at the edge of the corn to watch the sun go down
The switchback: a steep track, slippery with frost by six o'clock
Ingeborg's hand pump running at the top: the last running water on this side
encounters: The town
Shades of the guests on the slope (Shade stats), seventy of them, standing among the birches, facing downhill, waiting for supper
secrets: The town will not go down. It never has. Anyone who goes down the switchback at last light goes alone, or with the party.
A Crow Swarm rises from the oaks on the rim at sunset and circles the Hollow without a sound: a fear check DC 10 for a sign.

keyLocations.name: The Cold Hole
keyLocations.description: At the foot of the cold slope, among birches, a low wide mouth in the limestone, twelve feet across and four high, furred all round with frost an inch thick, breathing: out, a long plume of white vapour; in, a slow inhalation that pulls at your clothes and your hair. The ground in front of it is bare rock, frosted, with seventy years of lantern-oil stains where seven men stood in 1904. Inside, darkness, and cold beyond any winter, and somewhere far in, ice, and something that is not ice.
features: The rock floor where the houses stood in 1904: a half-circle of seven flat stones, worn smooth
The breath: out and in, faster as last light comes
Frost on everything, thickening by the minute
encounters: The Landlord (campaign controlFile)
The guests' Shades, in the cave mouth, in their good clothes
secrets: THE SURRENDER (Rule Four): at last light (from 6:21 p.m. until the last of the light leaves the sky at about 6:48: give the readers five or six rounds of reading, a round each and a round for the Landlord between), a living member of each of the seven houses stands on their house's stone and reads their house's line from the Book's first page aloud. The Landlord fights it (see the scene The Reading). If every house reads, the Cold Hole breathes out one last time and does not breathe in. The frost on the rocks runs as water. The Shades turn, one by one, and are not there. Every character present drops to Dread 0 (a creature laid to rest).

THE PAYING OUT (Rule Four): Harald Haugen, the hand that writes the names, strikes the guest's name in the Book, sets the Book on the Haugen stone, and walks into the Cold Hole. It is his choice, made in the moment. The breath goes in, long, and does not come out again. The Shades are gone. The lease is paid.
THE RENT PAID: if neither, the guest walks in at last light (Calling the Guest), and the breath goes in, and out, and the town on the rim goes home.

synopsis: Harvest Days. On Friday, while the parade goes down Main Street with Elsie Brandvold as Harvest Queen and the co-op's new grain dryer on a flatbed, the party goes house by house for the seven speakers the surrender needs: Ingeborg Vaage, who has waited seventy years; Harald Haugen or his son Rolf; Elsie or Arvid Brandvold; Gary Kubicek, the saved child, who must be told what saved him; Kjell Lunde, against his mother; Lillian Fossum, against her husband; and for the family that left, Sylvie Aldahl, or Einar, who crosses the Mississippi on Emil Pospisil's bus for the first time in twenty-three years. On Saturday the town is kind to its guest of honour, a player character whose name Harald inked in the Book after Dawn got out, and tries all day, very gently, to get one slice of Harvest Supper bread into them. At six the Channel 8 news van goes live from the fairgrounds, and the party can put the Book on television, which will bring the sheriff and the state and end Hollow Fork's secret, though not its bargain. At 6:10 the town walks out to the rim to see the sunset with the guest at its head, and at last light the Landlord calls its guest down the switchback to the Cold Hole. There, in the cold, with seventy guests' Shades in the cave mouth, seven people from seven houses try to read the lease back while the thing in the Hollow speaks to each of them in the voice of what it gave them. If they all hold, the Cold Hole breathes out and does not breathe in, and that night the frost comes to Hollow Fork and the luck is over. If the surrender fails, Harald Haugen may take the second door himself. If nobody does anything, the rent is paid. Sunday is the church bell, and what the town has become.
hook: Friday 11 October, 9 a.m. The high school band is tuning up at the end of Main Street. Somebody has hung a red kerchief on the door of every motel unit. On the guest's pillow there is a ribbon rosette, red and gold, that says GUEST OF HONOR, and a note in Elsie's hand: 'We saved you a seat at the head table. Please come. E.' Thirty-three hours to last light.

conclusions.conclusion: The surrender needs a living member of every house, by blood or marriage, at the Cold Hole at last light, reading their own line
clues: 4a: the Book's first page and Gunnar Haugen's clause, 'by blood or by marriage' (hs-scenario-003)
4b: Rev. Penrose's register: 'by every house that signed it, at the place where it was made, reading back their own names' (hs-scenario-002)
4d: Ingeborg, who heard it: 'every house that set its name to it unsays it here' (hs-scenario-003)
4c: Einar Aldahl: 'every house together, all seven, at the hole where they made it, and read it back' (hs-scenario-002)

conclusions.conclusion: The guest must be kept from walking down alone; refusing the Harvest Supper bread weakens the call
clues: 1a: the Book's 'took supper' column, blank for 1974 until the guest eats (the co-op safe, hs-scenario-002)
1b: the Furrow, 1904: the guest 'urged to partake of the new bread' (Madison, hs-scenario-002)
The town's plan and its gentle insistence on one slice (Rolf, Elsie, channel 14)
Calling the Guest: a friend holding them, or saying their real name and home, helps (Ingeborg; Old Lore)

conclusions.conclusion: Every ending costs something: the harvest and the town's luck, a man's life, or a guest
clues: Einar Aldahl: 'two doors out, and they both cost' (hs-scenario-002)
1951: the only year the rent went unpaid, the frost came and the corn died (the Book, the aerial photograph)
Marit Lunde: 'a hundred and forty families in that vault' (the bank)

acts.title: Friday: Seven Houses
acts.description: The parade, and the persuasion. While the town celebrates, the party goes after its speakers. Track the seven houses openly on a sheet (Elsie's order pad will do): each house is WON, WAVERING or LOST. Ingeborg is won already, and so is the Haugen house if Harald or Rolf agreed in hs-scenario-003. The point of this act is that the end of the bargain is a social achievement: people the players like have to give up something real, out loud, and the party has to ask them to.
objectives: Win a speaker for each of the seven houses: Vaage, Haugen, Brandvold, Kubicek, Lunde, Fossum, Aldahl
Bring Einar Aldahl over the river, or decide that Sylvie will speak for the Aldahls
Keep the guest safe, fed on the party's own food, and out of the town's gentle hands

scenes.name: The Parade
scenes.description: Friday morning, Main Street. The parade passes: the band, the fire truck, the floats, the antique tractors, the co-op's grain dryer, and Elsie Brandvold in a paper crown on the back of a convertible, waving and crying. The guest is given a seat of honour on the reviewing stand outside the bank, between Marit Lunde and Arnie Fossum, and offered a brat on a bun every half hour. While the town watches the parade, the party can work the houses. ELSIE AND ORRIN: Arvid is won the moment anyone asks him ('I'd give them back, the fifteen years'); Elsie comes if Arvid does, and if someone tells her that the young women in Unit 6 did not go anywhere peaceful (Persuasion DC 12, or Dawn herself, if she is safe and willing to come back to the edge of town and speak to Elsie across the creek). LILLIAN AND ARNIE: Lillian is won if anyone asks her alone (she has been waiting); telling Arnie is her choice, and she does it in the pie tent, and Arnie walks out without a word, and comes back an hour later and sits with his sons, and does not stop her. KJELL AND MARIT: see keyLocations; Kjell is won with Persuasion DC 12, and asks the party to stand behind him while he tells his mother, and Marit's face when he does is the hardest thing in the campaign.
scenes.readAloud: The band comes first, thirty kids in purple and gold playing the Washington Post march not quite together, and then the fire truck with its siren whooping and the firemen throwing Tootsie Rolls, and then the floats: the 4-H, the Legion, the Community Church with Pastor Tove waving from a hay wagon looking as if she would rather be anywhere else, the Ridge Inn softball team, a tractor from 1916, a tractor from 1928, a tractor from 1937, and the co-op's new grain dryer, a great silver cylinder on a flatbed with a banner: 70 GOOD YEARS — HERE'S TO 70 MORE. And then a white Chevrolet convertible with its top down and, sitting up on the back of it in a paper crown and a sash that says HARVEST QUEEN, Elsie Brandvold, waving to everyone she has ever fed, with tears running down her face. The crowd cheers for her. They cheer and cheer. Beside you on the reviewing stand, Arnie Fossum puts a hand on your shoulder, warm and heavy, and says, "Isn't it something? Isn't it something, though?"

skillChecks.success: One house won (the GM marks it on the sheet): Arvid and then Elsie for the Brandvolds; Lillian for the Fossums; Kjell for the Lundes. Each takes a scene, and each costs the speaker something in front of the people they love. Roll once per house, at advantage with the right evidence (the back room, the Book, Dawn's Polaroids, the stones).
skillChecks.failure: The house wavers. The speaker says they need to think, and will tell you at the supper. Mark it WAVERING: at the rim, a WAVERING speaker comes if someone they trust walks beside them (Insight DC 12 to know who).

skillChecks.success: Who is breaking and who is holding: Elsie is breaking toward you; Arnie is breaking, and does not know which way; Marit is not breaking at all; Dr. Kubicek broke years ago and has been standing anyway. You know which speaker needs which friend beside them at the Cold Hole.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is smiling. You cannot tell who is with you.

skillChecks.success: You get the guest off the reviewing stand and away from Arnie's hand without a scene, with a story about a bathroom and a sick stomach, and the town lets them go, because the town is polite. For an hour nobody is offering them food.
skillChecks.failure: Arnie says, 'I'll walk with you,' and does. He means it kindly. He is not letting go.

scenes.name: Gary
scenes.description: Friday afternoon, Gary Kubicek's clinic, between a calving and a dog with a cut paw. He has to be told (see keyLocations). Persuasion DC 15, at advantage with the Book's 1958 line or with his father in the room. If his father is there, Arlen Kubicek confirms it all in a voice nobody has heard from him before, and then sits on the kennel bench and does not say anything else. Gary goes outside and stands in the alley for a long time. When he comes back: 'I've had sixteen years. They had none. I'll read it.' And then, because he is a vet and practical: 'What happens to me, after?' Nobody knows. The rules say nothing. Let the players answer honestly. If Gary will not, Dr. Arlen can be won instead only by Gary asking him to. The Kubiceks are the house most likely to be WAVERING at the rim.
scenes.readAloud: The clinic smells of disinfectant and wet dog. There are crayon drawings taped to the door of the kennel run: a horse, a cow, a man in a white coat with a stethoscope, labelled DADDY. Gary Kubicek is a big sunburned man of twenty-six with his sleeves rolled up and a border collie on the steel table, stitching its paw, talking to it the whole time, "Good girl, good girl, almost done." On the wall behind him, in a cheap frame, there is a page from a medical journal: AN UNEXPLAINED REMISSION OF ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA IN A TEN-YEAR-OLD MALE, 1959. He sees you looking at it and grins. "That's me. I'm famous at the Mayo Clinic. Dad gave me that on my twenty-first birthday. Never would say why." He ties off the last stitch and lifts the dog down and looks at you, and stops grinning. "You're the people from the corn. What do you want with me?"

skillChecks.success: Gary hears it. All of it. He goes out into the alley. When he comes back, he says he will read for the Kubiceks. House won. He asks you to tell nobody until the supper, so he can tell Carol himself.
skillChecks.failure: Gary says you are sick people, and that his father is the finest man he knows, and asks you to leave. But that night he goes to his father and asks him, and his father tells him. Mark the house WAVERING.

skillChecks.success: You can tell Gary the truth as a medical person: remissions like his happen, very rarely, without any reason anyone can find. Nobody can say whether his was the bargain or luck. The not-knowing is the thing he has to choose with. It helps him, a little, to hear it said straight.
skillChecks.failure: You do not know what to tell him about his own body, and he can see that.

skillChecks.success: Gary is not afraid of dying. He is afraid of the girls growing up in a town that did this, and of being the reason. Tell him it ends with him, and he will do it.
skillChecks.failure: A big, friendly man who has just been told the worst thing he will ever hear.

scenes.name: Over the Big Water
scenes.description: Friday, Winona and the high bridge. If Sylvie or the party fetches Einar (see keyLocations), the crossing is the scene: Einar in the back of a car or on Emil Pospisil's eastbound bus, his father's kerchief in his fist, the Mississippi half a mile wide under the steel span, and his fear check DC 15 (advantage with Sylvie beside him). On the Wisconsin side he is quiet for an hour, and then talks the whole way, about his father and the farm and the night of the Fork bridge, and about Signe, whom he loved too, a little, when they were young. In Hollow Fork, the town sees him get off the bus outside the Fork Diner, and the whole of Main Street stops. Ingeborg comes down from the rim in her gumboots, and the two old people stand in the street and look at each other, and Einar says, 'Inga,' and she says, 'Einar. You came back.' If Einar will not come, Sylvie speaks for the Aldahls; play her scene at the stone house with Ingeborg, who gives her Signe's place at the table.
scenes.readAloud: The Greyhound comes off the high bridge onto the Wisconsin shore at ten to eleven with the sun on the river behind it, and the old man in the third row with the red kerchief in his fist has not breathed, as far as anyone can tell, for the whole half mile. He breathes now, a long ragged breath, and looks out of the window at the bluffs and the black frozen corn going by, and says, to nobody, "Same as it was." An hour later the bus comes over the watershed ridge, and the corn on the far side of the road is green, and he puts his hand flat against the glass. When Emil pulls up outside the Fork Diner at 11:40, the parade has just ended, and Main Street is full of people, and every one of them turns to see who is getting off a bus the town cancelled. An old man with a cane climbs down. The street goes silent, all the way to the elevator.

skillChecks.success: Einar comes. House of Aldahl won, with Einar to read it, or Sylvie, or both together.
skillChecks.failure: Einar will not cross. He gives Sylvie his father's kerchief and says, 'You read it, then. You're an Aldahl. Read it for all of us.' House of Aldahl won, with Sylvie to read it.

skillChecks.success: Einar is frightened, and glad, and ashamed of being glad, and in love with being back; he has missed Hollow Fork every day for twenty-three years. That is what the bargain cost him.
skillChecks.failure: An old man on a bus.

skillChecks.success: Sylvie (or anyone) gets the old man talking and laughing on the long drive: a story, a song from the forties, a card trick. He arrives in Hollow Fork with his back straight.
skillChecks.failure: He sits in silence the whole way, knuckles white on his cane.

encounters: None hostile. The town is everywhere, kind and watchful, and Arnie's men keep close to the guest

If Dawn was caught in hs-scenario-003: getting her out of Dr. Kubicek's clinic on Friday (two townsmen, Frightened Townsman stats, and Dr. Kubicek, who will let her go if Gary asks him) and to Emil's 4:10 bus

acts.title: Saturday: The Supper
acts.description: The festival's great day, and the town's last attempt. The point of this act is keeping the guest alive and out of the Landlord's call until the speakers can reach the Cold Hole, and deciding what to do with the cameras. The town wants the guest at the head table, fed and toasted; the party wants them anywhere else. The town walks to the rim at 6:10. The Landlord calls at last light.
objectives: Keep the guest from eating the Harvest Supper bread, or limit the damage
Decide whether to put the Book on live television at six
Get the seven speakers, the Book and the guest to the rim at last light, and down the switchback

scenes.name: The Pie Auction
scenes.description: Saturday, the tractor pull at ten (Ward or Rolf can enter; the co-op's own pickup pulls a sled of four tons the length of the track; it is very loud and very funny), and the pie auction at two in the pavilion, where Elsie's rhubarb pie goes for $140 to Arnie Fossum, who gives it to the guest. All day, the town tries, kindly, to feed the guest the Harvest Supper bread (see keyLocations): a sandwich, a slice of bread with the first-grain butter, a toast at the supper at five where the guest's place has a loaf on the plate. Refusing politely every time is a Persuasion or Deception check DC 12 (each failure, the guest eats something; the bread itself only at the supper). Marit Lunde, if Kjell has told her, finds the party at the pie tent and makes her last offer: $5,000 each, in cash, from the bank's own vault, to take the guest and go, now, over the water, tonight, and never come back. 'The rent will be paid. Somebody will be passing through. Somebody always is.' It is a real offer. It is the Rent Paid ending with money in it. Let the players feel it.
scenes.readAloud: The pavilion is full: six hundred people at long tables under strings of bulbs, the smell of ham and scalloped potatoes and coffee, children running between the tables, a fiddle somewhere, and on every table a basket of bread, golden, thick-crusted, still warm, the first loaves from the first grain of the 1974 harvest. At the head table under the banner, between the Harvest Queen in her paper crown and the co-op manager in his good grey suit, there is an empty chair, and on the plate in front of it a whole round loaf with a red kerchief tied round it like a ribbon. Everyone in the pavilion knows whose chair it is. Every now and then, someone at a table turns to look at the door to see if the guest has come. They are smiling. A woman you have never met comes up to the guest with a slice on a napkin, buttered thick, and says, "You must be hungry, hon, you haven't eaten all day. Just a bite. For luck."

skillChecks.success: The guest refuses, kindly, every time, and the town lets it go every time, a little more frightened each time. By five, the guest has eaten nothing of Hollow Fork's today. At last light they have advantage on every WIS save against Calling the Guest.
skillChecks.failure: A bite, for luck. The bread is the best thing you have ever tasted. Someone writes 'took supper 10/12/74' on a napkin and runs it up to the co-op office. The call will be strong.

skillChecks.success: Marit Lunde's offer is real, and she hates herself for making it, and she would make it again. She does not think the surrender can work. She thinks that if it does, she will watch a hundred and forty families lose their farms in the next ten years, and she is right.
skillChecks.failure: A banker offering you money to go away. It is a lot of money.

skillChecks.success: At the tractor pull, whoever drives the co-op pickup pulls the sled the full three hundred feet, and the town goes wild, and for twenty minutes the strangers are heroes. Arnie Fossum shakes their hand and does not let go, and says, 'You're all right. You know that? You're all right,' and means it.
skillChecks.failure: The pickup bogs at two hundred feet in a cloud of black smoke. Everyone laughs, kindly. Someone brings you a beer, and a sandwich.

scenes.name: Live at Six
scenes.description: Six o'clock, the Channel 8 van by the bandstand. Bonnie Sedlak goes live for the six o'clock news across western Wisconsin and southeastern Minnesota: 'the town the frost forgot celebrates seventy good years'. Xavier Boone, if he is a companion, is on the camera and will point it wherever the party asks. The choice: put the Book, the back room, the luggage tags and Dawn's Polaroids on live television, or not. If they do, Bonnie (who sees the story of her career) goes with it, Marit Lunde walks to the van to stop it and is too late, and the broadcast reaches Sheriff Dahlquist eating his supper in Linden Falls, who calls the State Patrol and drives out over the ridge, arriving at the Fork bridge at 7:30 (after last light, too late for the Cold Hole, in time for everything afterwards). The secret is out from that moment, whatever else happens: the keepers face the law and the newspapers, and Hollow Fork becomes a story told on the radio for years. The television does not touch the Landlord; it has no church and no audience and does not care. If the party does not use the cameras, the secret can be kept, at least for now. Either way, at 6:10 the town gets up from the tables and begins to walk out to the rim, and the guest's chair is empty or not.
scenes.readAloud: The red light on top of the camera comes on. Bonnie Sedlak, in her camel coat with a red kerchief somebody gave her at the throat, smiles into the lens and says, "Good evening from Hollow Fork, where tonight the whole town has turned out to celebrate seventy years of good harvests, in a fall when the frost has taken so much from so many..." Behind her the pavilion is emptying. Six hundred people are getting up from the tables and putting on their coats and moving out toward the road, the families and the old couples and the teenagers, quietly, all in the same direction, south, toward the corn and the rim of the Hollow, where the sun is going down red. Behind the camera, Xavier Boone looks up from the eyepiece, and looks at you, and lifts his eyebrows: well?

skillChecks.success: Bonnie takes the Book and the Polaroids from you on air without missing a beat, and reads the first line of the 1974 entry aloud into the camera, and the people of western Wisconsin hear it at their supper tables. Hollow Fork's secret is over. The sheriff is coming.
skillChecks.failure: Bonnie hesitates, and the station cuts to a commercial, and when it comes back she is doing the weather. She will run it at ten, if you give her a reason. The town has seen you try.

skillChecks.success: Watching the crowd go: half the town is walking to the rim because it always has, and half because it wants to see what happens, and some of them, here and there, are walking with their heads down and their kerchiefs in their pockets. Not everyone in Hollow Fork wants the rent paid tonight.
skillChecks.failure: Six hundred people walking south into the sunset, all together, without a word.

skillChecks.success: If you would rather not use the cameras: you get the Book away from the van and down the Fossum lane ahead of the crowd without anyone stopping you, and the secret stays with the seven houses, for now.
skillChecks.failure: Arnie's men are between you and the lane. They step aside when you walk up to them. But they see what you have.

scenes.name: The Walk to the Rim
scenes.description: 6:10 to 6:21 p.m. The town walks out the Fossum lane between the walls of corn to the rim, six hundred people, a fiddle playing, nobody talking. At the rim they stand in the stubble along the edge of the corn and watch the sun go down over the Hollow. The guest, if they are with the town, is at the front, between Arnie and Marit (or whoever has taken their places). The speakers must break from the crowd: each one walking out of the line of their neighbours and families to the head of the switchback, in front of everyone, is the cost of it; a WON speaker comes; a WAVERING speaker comes only if someone they trust walks with them (or a Chaplain's Steady Now, or the right word). Ingeborg goes first. Then: at 6:21, the sun's rim touches the ridge, and below, the Cold Hole breathes out a great plume of white, and the Landlord calls its guest (Calling the Guest, campaign controlFile): the guest must make a WIS save DC 15 each round or walk toward the switchback; advantage if they did not eat the bread today, or if a friend holds them, or says their real name and home. Anyone holding a guest who is walking is dragged along unless they pass a STR check DC 12. The town on the rim does not move. The party must go down the switchback to the Cold Hole now, with the speakers, with the Book, with or without the guest. The guest is safest held at the top by the running pump (Rule Two: the pump's water across the lane is a wall; the call still pulls, but the Landlord cannot come up to take them past it); or the guest can be taken down with the party, which is braver and worse.
scenes.readAloud: The sun goes down red over the ridges on the far side of the Hollow, and the whole town of Hollow Fork stands along the rim in the stubble to watch it, six hundred people in a line, in their good coats and their red kerchiefs, nobody saying a word. The fiddle stops. Below, in the coulee, the shadows come up the slopes like water filling a basin, and the birches go grey, and the old church on its bench goes dark, and at the foot of the cold slope the Cold Hole breathes out a plume of white higher than the trees, and holds it, and draws it back in, so long and so deep that the leaves on the rim stir toward it and the corn behind you leans. And in the crowd, someone you know takes a step forward, toward the head of the switchback, with an odd, gentle, puzzled look on their face, as if somebody had called their name from very far away, in a voice they loved.

skillChecks.success: A WAVERING speaker steps out of the line of their family and walks to the head of the switchback, and the people beside them let them go. (One check per wavering speaker; advantage if the right person walks with them.)
skillChecks.failure: The speaker cannot move. Their wife has their hand, or their mother, or their own fear. Someone else of that house must be found in the crowd, now, or the house is LOST.

skillChecks.success: You hold the guest. Arms round them from behind, heels dug in, saying their name and the name of their home over and over, while they pull toward the switchback like a dog on a leash, gently, smiling, not understanding. They do not go. (Each round: the guest's WIS save DC 15, with advantage while held.)
skillChecks.failure: The guest walks, and you are dragged, boots skidding on frost, to the head of the switchback. Someone else has to help.

skillChecks.success: Across the crowd, Harald Haugen is watching his son at the head of the switchback with the Book in his hands. He has the face of a man who has just made up his mind.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is looking down into the Hollow. Nobody is looking at anyone else.

encounters: None hostile: the town does not stop the speakers and does not go down. Arnie Fossum's men stand between the crowd and the head of the switchback, and step aside for anyone who walks up to them
The Landlord's call (Calling the Guest) from 6:21: WIS saves DC 15 for the guest each round
A Crow Swarm rising silent from the oaks on the rim: a fear check DC 10

acts.title: Last Light: The Cold Hole
acts.description: The end of the bargain, or not. The party and the speakers go down the switchback in the last light with the cold coming up, through seventy Shades standing among the birches, to the Cold Hole, and read. The Landlord fights the reading with cold and with offers. The point of this act is the cost: whatever ends here, the players should know what it cost and who paid.
objectives: Get the speakers and the Book down the switchback to the Cold Hole before the light goes
Hold each speaker steady through the reading while the Landlord speaks to them
End it, by the surrender or the paying out; or live with the rent paid

scenes.name: Down the Switchback
scenes.description: 6:21 to about 6:30. Half a mile down the switchback in failing light, frost forming on the track as they go (Acrobatics DC 10 or fall, 1d6 bludgeoning, and someone has to help an old person up; Ingeborg is eighty-two and Einar seventy-nine and they will not be carried). Among the birches on either side, the Shades of seventy guests, in their good clothes from seventy years, stand facing downhill, waiting for supper: a fear check DC 15 (13 with the rules known; 17 in darkness); they do not move unless someone speaks to them, and then they turn and say 'Is it time?' A Chaplain or anyone with Graveside can tell them it nearly is. The cold comes up the slope to meet the party. Halfway down, the light goes out (once per scenario): every flashlight and lantern dies at once. Fire still works: a match, a flare, a kerosene bottle; and draws it. At the bottom, the Cold Hole: breathing faster, white plumes higher than the trees, frost an inch thick on every rock, the seven flat stones in a half-circle in front of it.
scenes.readAloud: You go down into the Hollow as the light goes out of it. The switchback is a farm track gone to moss and leaf-litter, steep, turning back on itself among the trees, and frost is forming on it as you walk, on the leaves, on the stones, on the hems of your coats, faster than you can believe, white feathers growing across the path ahead of you as if the cold were laying a carpet for you. The birches stand white in the dusk on either side. And among them, between them, people. Standing still. Men in brown suits and women in good wool coats, a young man in an Army jacket from 1946, a hunter in a red vest, a salesman with a sample case, a young woman in a sundress from some summer before the war, all of them facing downhill, all of them pale as the birch bark, all of them waiting, patiently, the way people wait outside a church hall for the doors to open for a supper. Seventy of them. None of them looks at you. Below, at the bottom of the coulee, a white breath goes up into the dark, and is drawn back down, and the trees lean.

skillChecks.success: Down the frosted switchback without a fall, with an old person on your arm.
skillChecks.failure: Your feet go out from under you on the frost. 1d6 bludgeoning, and the Book, if you are carrying it, slides away down the slope toward the Shades; someone has to go and get it.

skillChecks.success: You say to the Shades, gently, that the supper is nearly over, and they can go home soon. One by one, those nearest the path turn their faces toward you, and something in them eases. They will not trouble the readers. (A Chaplain's Graveside gives advantage.)
skillChecks.failure: They turn to you, all of them at once, seventy faces, and say 'Is it time?', and the fear check is at disadvantage.

skillChecks.success: When the lights die, you keep the path by feel, the slope under one hand, counting turns, and bring everyone down to the coulee floor together.
skillChecks.failure: In the dark someone takes a wrong turn and ends up on the cold slope above the Cold Hole, among the broken rocks, with the breath coming up between the stones under their feet. They will find the bottom, but separately, and late.

scenes.name: The Reading
scenes.description: The surrender (Rule Four). Each speaker stands on their house's stone in the half-circle and reads their house's line from the Book's first page (Harald, Rolf or the party holds the Book for them, with a light, which is warm, and draws it). Run it as rounds: each round, one speaker reads; between readings, the Landlord acts. It does two things. It breathes: the Long Breath at the half-circle (CON save DC 14, half damage on success; anyone hiding their breath is unaffected, but you cannot read aloud and hide your breath at once, and that is the cruelty of it; the party can stand in front of the readers, take the breath for them, hold kerchiefs over their mouths between lines). And it speaks: to the next reader, in the voice of what it gave them. To Elsie or Arvid, in Arvid's own voice from 1959, from the hospital bed: 'Elsie, don't let me go.' To Gary, in his father's voice: 'You lived because of me.' To Lillian, in Arnie's voice, asking her what will become of the boys. To Kjell, in his mother's. To Ingeborg, in her mother's, as it spoke in 1904. To Einar or Sylvie, in Signe's. To Harald or Rolf, in Anna Haugen's. Each reader makes a WIS save DC 13 to read their line through (advantage if someone stands beside them, holds them, says their name; a Chaplain's Steady Now; a Faithful character's Something to Hold On To lent as a hand on the shoulder grants nothing mechanical but the GM may allow advantage). A reader who fails falters and stops; another member of the same house present can take up the line next round; if none can, the house is LOST and the surrender fails, and the Landlord knows it was tried. If all seven houses read before the last light leaves the sky (five or six rounds; the GM counts openly), the Cold Hole breathes out once, long, and does not breathe in. The frost on the rocks turns to water and runs. The Shades are gone. Every character present drops to Dread 0.
scenes.readAloud: Ingeborg goes first, because she said she would. She steps up onto the flat stone at the end of the half-circle in her gumboots, eighty-two years old, with the Book held open in front of her by a young man with a flashlight, and the cold pouring out of the cave mouth over her like a river, frosting her white hair whiter, and she reads in a high, clear, old voice: "I, of the house of Vaage, that set its name hereto, unsay it." And the cave mouth breathes in. Long. The whole Hollow leans toward it, the trees, the frost, your coats, your hair, the breath out of your mouths. And then, out of the dark of the cave, in a woman's voice, warm, weak, from a sickbed, a voice none of you has ever heard and every one of you knows: "Inga. Inga, sweetheart. Don't. I'll die. Don't let me die." The old woman on the stone shuts her eyes. Her lips move. And then she opens them, and says, louder, "Mother, you died in 1959, at ninety, in your bed, and I held your hand, and that was a good death and a long one, and it was bought with seventy strangers. I unsay it." She steps down. One.

skillChecks.success: You see which reader is going to break before they do, and are beside them when the voice comes, with a hand on their arm, saying their name. They have advantage on the WIS save.
skillChecks.failure: The voice comes, and you were watching the cave, not the reader.

skillChecks.success: A reader has faltered on their stone, the Book shaking in front of them, the voice of their dead or their living calling them from the dark. You get to them, and say the true thing, and they find their place in the line and read it through. (Lets a faltering reader try the save again next round.)
skillChecks.failure: The reader steps down off the stone, weeping. If there is no one else of that house here, the house is lost, and the surrender with it. Look to Harald.

skillChecks.success: Between breaths, you keep the old ones and the frostbitten on their feet: rub hands, breathe warmth into them, a Physician's Steady Hands. Nobody falls before their line.
skillChecks.failure: Einar (or Ingeborg) goes down on the frost after reading, grey-lipped, and must be carried out, or die of the cold in the next half hour.

scenes.name: After
scenes.description: The ending, whichever it is (campaign controlFile outcomes). THE SURRENDER: the Cold Hole stops breathing. Up on the rim, the town feels the cold go; six hundred people standing in the stubble feel the air turn ordinary, chilly, October; and the first of them begin to cry. The party climbs out of the Hollow in the dark to a town that does not know what to do with them. That night, at about two in the morning, the frost the rest of the Midwest had on 23 September comes over the ridge and down the coulees and takes Hollow Fork's standing corn, half the harvest, in an hour; the town wakes on Sunday to black fields. The sheriff and the State Patrol, if the cameras rolled, are at the Fork bridge by dawn. THE PAYING OUT: if the surrender failed, or before it can fail, Harald Haugen takes the Book from whoever is holding it, strikes the guest's name with his own hand, lays the Book on the Haugen stone, says 'Rolf. It's all right,' and walks into the Cold Hole. Do not describe what happens to him; fade at the mouth. The breath goes in, long, and does not come out. The Shades are gone. The frost does not come that night; the harvest stands; the luck is over from tomorrow. Rolf is twenty-four and the manager of a co-op. THE RENT PAID: if neither, the guest walks down at last light (or Dawn, or someone passing through), and the breath goes in and out, and the town goes home, and Ingeborg sets a stone. EPILOGUE, Sunday 13 October: the Community Church bell at nine; Pastor Tove's sermon, if she is alive and here, on whatever the players' choices have earned; the grain dryers silent or roaring; Emil's bus going through on Tuesday, and stopping, and somebody getting on; and one last image of the fields from the ridge road: black, or green.
scenes.readAloud: Sunday morning. The bell of the Community Church rings across Hollow Fork at nine, as it has every Sunday since 1906, and from the ridge road where County Road K crosses the divide you can see the whole of it: the elevator, the village, the farms on their ridgetops, the line of the creek, and the Hollow, a dark fold in the land to the south. The air is cold and clean and smells of woodsmoke. It is an ordinary October morning in western Wisconsin. Down in the village, people are walking to church in their good coats. Not one of them is wearing a red kerchief. And the fields, the four hundred acres of the Fossum corn and every field on the ridgetops around it, from the ridge road to the creek, are...

skillChecks.success: Whatever the ending, you see what the town feels: grief, relief, rage, shame, and under all of it, for some of them, something like freedom. They will never forgive you. Some of them will thank you, years from now, quietly, in a letter.
skillChecks.failure: The town is a closed door. You will not be welcome here again.

skillChecks.success: If the sheriff has come: you give Clifford Dahlquist what he asked for, a piece of paper a jury would look at, the Book and the back room and the stones and Dawn's statement, and he takes his hat off in the co-op back room, and says 'God help me, I looked,' and calls the state. What the law makes of seventy years is for the GM and the epilogue.
skillChecks.failure: The sheriff takes statements and says it will be a long time sorting out, and that nobody in Linden Falls will ever believe the half of it.

skillChecks.success: Gary Kubicek, a week later, gets his blood drawn at the clinic in Linden Falls, and the results are normal, and he laughs out loud in the parking lot. The rules said nothing about him. The GM never adds a rule.
skillChecks.failure: Gary does not get tested. He says he does not want to know. He coaches his daughters' softball team in the spring, and every time he gets a cold Carol watches him.

encounters: The Landlord at the Cold Hole (campaign controlFile): it fights the reading with the Long Breath and its voices, Frost Touch on anyone who stands between it and a reader, and Calling the Guest on its guest; it cannot be destroyed by damage, and driving it back with fire or running water buys a round, not a victory
Seventy Shades among the birches (Shade stats), waiting; they are a horror, not an attack, unless someone tries to drag one to the cave or takes the Book among them
If the guest came down: the call at the cave mouth is DC 17, and a guest who reaches the mouth goes in unless held by two people

npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Vaage; first
npcsInvolved.description: In gumboots on a frosted stone, reading in a high clear voice.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see it end before she dies.

npcsInvolved.name: Harald Haugen, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Haugen; the hand that writes the names
npcsInvolved.description: In his good grey suit at the supper and at the rim; the second door.

npcsInvolved.name: Rolf Haugen, 24
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Haugen; companion
npcsInvolved.description: Holding the Book and the flashlight for the readers.

npcsInvolved.name: Elsie and Arvid Brandvold, 61 and 67
npcsInvolved.role: Speakers for the house of Brandvold
npcsInvolved.description: The Harvest Queen in a paper crown, and the baker who would give back his fifteen years.

npcsInvolved.name: Gary Kubicek, 26
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Kubicek; the saved child, grown
npcsInvolved.description: A big sunburned vet with crayon drawings on his kennel door.
npcsInvolved.motivation: 'I've had sixteen years. They had none.'

npcsInvolved.name: Dr. Arlen Kubicek, 66
npcsInvolved.description: Standing behind his son with his hands on his shoulders.

npcsInvolved.name: Kjell Lunde, 30
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Lunde
npcsInvolved.description: The bank's loan officer, kerchief in his pocket, an unsent application to a Minneapolis bank.

npcsInvolved.name: Marit Lunde, 54
npcsInvolved.description: Making her last offer in the pie tent: $5,000 each, in cash.

npcsInvolved.name: Lillian Fossum, 46
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Fossum, by marriage

npcsInvolved.motivation: Twenty-four years of being afraid on Labor Day.

npcsInvolved.name: Arnie Fossum, 49
npcsInvolved.description: Standing between the crowd and the switchback; stepping aside.

npcsInvolved.name: Einar Aldahl, 79
npcsInvolved.role: Speaker for the house of Aldahl
npcsInvolved.description: Off Emil's bus on Main Street with his father's kerchief in his fist.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have done it once and for all, this time.

npcsInvolved.name: Emil Pospisil, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Stopping where he has been told not to, engine running.

npcsInvolved.name: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Arriving at the Fork bridge at 7:30 if the cameras rolled.

rewards.money: There is no payment for this. Marit Lunde's $5,000 each is on offer to a party that takes the guest and leaves without ending it, and is the price of the Rent Paid. Quentin Talbert's story, if the secret comes out, runs in the Courier-Ledger and is picked up by the wire, and earns him a raise and a book contract; Bonnie Sedlak gets a job at a Minneapolis station; Yolanda Ibarra's dissertation has a chapter she will never be able to publish as fact. Dawn Petrakis sends Tess the money she owed her, $60, in a card that says 'Thank you for not answering the phone. I mean it. If you had, I wouldn't have called the second time, and you wouldn't have come.' (She never called a second time. Tess will think about that for the rest of her life.)
items: The Book, given to the law, or to the State Historical Society, or burned on the co-op's back step by Rolf Haugen, or kept
A red kerchief for each, which none of them will ever wear again and none of them will throw away
Ingeborg's last stone, if the bargain ends: she sets it on Sunday afternoon at the end of the row, a little apart, with no space after it
A Polaroid from Dawn's camera of the seven readers on their stones, taken by somebody at the last moment, a flare of white in the middle of it
A Greyhound ticket from Hollow Fork to anywhere, paid for by Emil Pospisil

twists: Marit Lunde is right. If the surrender works, the luck ends, and when the farm crisis comes in the 1980s Hollow Fork will lose a third of its farms like every other town on the ridge. The campaign's best ending costs the people the players came to like the thing they loved most. The GM should say so in the epilogue, plainly.

Harald Haugen's choice is his own, and he may make it even if the surrender is succeeding: if the Landlord's voice breaks Rolf on the Haugen stone, Harald steps up, takes the Book from his son, and reads the Haugen line himself instead, and the reading goes on. A good man can choose the first door at the last minute too.

The Landlord keeps its terms exactly, to the end. If the surrender works, it goes. It does not curse anyone, it does not take anyone on the way out, and it does not come back. It was never evil in any way it would understand. That should be the most frightening thing in the campaign.

Nothing in the rules says the bargain's end takes back what it gave. Mrs. Vaage died at ninety; Arvid's heart and Gary's blood are their own now. The players will not know that at the Cold Hole, and neither will the readers; they choose anyway. The GM never adds a rule.
dmTips: Before the last session, check in with the players about the content (dread.json running_horror). The Reading puts the voices of the dead and the dying in the Landlord's mouth; if a player says 'skip that', cut to the next reader and keep going.

Track the seven houses openly: WON, WAVERING, LOST. Every house has more than one possible speaker (by blood or by marriage), so a party that works hard can win all seven on Friday. The hardest are the Kubiceks and the Lundes; plan for one of them to be WAVERING at the rim.

The guest is a player character (or Dawn, or Pastor Tove). Calling the Guest is a WIS save DC 15 each round from 6:21; advantage if they ate no Hollow Fork food today, or are held, or hear their real name and home. Holding them at the top by Ingeborg's running pump is safest; taking them down is braver. Never take control of the character; describe the pull and let the player play it.
The cameras end the secret, not the bargain. Make sure the players understand the difference; the Landlord has no audience.

The paying out is Harald's, and only Harald's. If the surrender fails, give him the moment; if a player tries to volunteer for the second door, remind them gently that the terms say the hand that writes the names, and that hand is his. Fade out at the cave mouth. Never describe what happens to him inside.

The light goes out once: on the switchback. After that, fire and the Book-holder's single flashlight (if the GM allows it back for the reading, because the reading needs a light) are all there is. A light is warm, and draws it, and the readers need one. That is the scene's cruelty and its courage.
Whatever the ending, give it its cost in the epilogue: black fields and a closed elevator, or Rolf alone in the co-op office, or a new stone. Then let the players talk about it.
Budget an hour and a half for Friday, an hour for Saturday until the walk, and an hour and a half for the Hollow and the epilogue.
